Rubicon report

Technology and young people's moods

Question In the 12 pilot interviews I04, I06, I07, I17, I18, I24, I28, I29, I37, I42, I43 and I48 (drawn at random within each borough and gender from the 48 interviews with young Londoners about loneliness), what different roles do the young people describe technology and social media playing in their own positive and negative moods, how many people describe each role, and on which side of mood?

The case is one person (one interview); a person can describe several roles, on both sides. A passage counts where the speaker ties a technology to a feeling of their own, positive or negative, including feeling lonely or feeling connected. Technology covers social media, messaging, phone and video calls, gaming, streaming and the internet generally. Any role counts: starting a feeling, keeping it going, easing it or lifting it. Feelings the interviewer suggests and the speaker does not take up, feelings of other people, and general remarks about social media or "people these days" that the speaker does not apply to themselves do not count. Accounts the interviewer prompted by raising technology count, but are marked, so the answer can say how many raised a role unprompted. The roles are drawn from the interviews: each passage is coded openly in the speaker's words, the labels are gathered into a short list of roles (a soft recode of the open coding, each passage read once), and the evaluator sees the list with an example passage for each before anything is counted by it. Every passage of the 12 interviews is read in full. The answer describes the roles, counted by person, with quotations, and gives no verdict. A fresh reader checks the answer against the passages it cites and the documents before it is shown (a check, not a blind recode). Separately from the answer, report anything in the documents that bears on the question but does not fit the frame it sets, each point once, in its own section, which the rest of the answer points to rather than repeats.

The answer

Across the interviews, the young people describe the following roles that technology plays in their own moods, counted by person.

Lifting or easing mood:

  • Keeping in touch with particular people by call, message, social media or a shared series (; without prompting, ).
  • Entertainment and distraction: YouTube, Netflix, phone and telly, console games, funny posts and music ().
  • Contact on their own terms, choosing when to talk or to log off ().
  • Comfort when lonely or low, mostly from music ().
  • Recognition from posting and motivation from pictures (, ).

Lowering mood:

  • Comparing themselves with others' lives, looks or luxury on screen ().
  • Screens that fail to fill empty time or leave them still alone ().
  • Fear of judgement keeping them off social media, or technology as the means of withdrawing ().
  • Seeing in posts that they were left out ().
  • Messages and calls that let them down ().
  • Phones and games coming between them and the people they are with ().
  • Dismay at social media's fakery ().
  • Being cut off without a phone (, ).

Most describe technology on both sides of their mood: people tie it to a feeling of their own that it lifts and to one that it lowers. people () describe it only lifting their mood, () only lowering it, and () never tie it to a feeling of their own.

Two patterns run through these roles. Contact with a particular person through a screen is told mostly as easing loneliness, though and describe messages and calls that hurt, while watching or playing alone is told both ways, as failing to fill the gap and as filling time or lifting mood (). Most of the negative accounts of social media are about the measure it holds up: others' better lives, and events the speaker was left out of; the others are fear of being judged (), dismay at its fakery (, ) and browsing that brings mood down () ().

What lifts mood

people describe technology lifting or easing their mood. Keeping in touch is the role raised most often without prompting (). A call makes being alone in their apartment less bad for one interviewee, though it is still the loneliest place: "it’s not as bad as living in Essex, because even when I’m in my apartment I have some things to do, like whether I’m on the phone with a friend" (). In their first year at university, on a doctor's advice, the same interviewee called home, and "it did help a little bit, not too much" (). Another recalls friends from university and sixth form who "lit you up when you felt so down or lonely, just a phone call away" (), and adds that "since I started working, you know, it’s not the same as before" (). Others call or message someone when bored of their own company (), know that they "could call one of my friends" (), or had family texts checking on them during exams ().

Entertainment is mostly screens used alone: one interviewee likes "going on YouTube and just watching stuff that I never think to learn" (), and another likes to "sit there and go on my phone and watch telly" (). Comfort is narrower: turning to music when lonely or low, to share and understand the feeling, in (), and to motivational YouTube videos, "whatever helps", in , in answer to a question that raised social media ().

For contact on their own terms (), the value is control. One interviewee says "being in bed with my phone it's like I can be myself and still be accepted" and "I can just log off, you know. When you're with people you cannot just walk away." (). Another is "quite careful with how I manage my social media, who I follow, who I talk to, so it's not an unpleasant feeling when I'm on social media, it's normally good" (). Recognition from posting Snapchat stories, and motivation from gym pictures, appear only in (); the same interviewee's second thoughts about posting are under Outside the frame.

What lowers mood

people describe technology starting, keeping going or worsening a bad feeling of their own. Comparison () is mostly about social media. Seeing others "all happy" on social media when already sad and lonely makes one interviewee feel worse: "Not worse, but it does a little bit" (). Another feels that people on Instagram are better: "I just almighty feel like they're better than me" (). A third "sometimes does get a bit jealousy" at luxury lives on Instagram and Facebook, and at once discounts it (). Outside social media, one penalises themselves each morning for not looking like "the models on TV" ().

Seeing that they were left out is close to comparison but about a particular event: photos of outings, when "you start feeling alone" (), or learning, on Facebook as far as they remember, that friends went out without them ().

Empty filler is the commonest negative role outside social media: "Sometimes, TV can be boring to watch, so you just turn it off" (). Of their first year at university, another says of watching YouTube alone: "But at the end of the day, you know, I’m still alone." ().

Fear of judgement and withdrawal keep loneliness going (). One interviewee keeps off Snapchat and Instagram for fear of being judged, which leaves them "forced to sort of keep myself to myself" (), and "that kind of sort of made me feel more lonely" (). Another texts excuses to stay in bed because "you’re scared of their opinion" (). A third used to doubt whether people would like their true self behind the character they had built on social media ().

Messages and calls let people down: the phone going off after a breakup and not being the ex (); "looking at your phone, waiting for an invitation" that "just doesn't come through" (), which the same interviewee then qualifies (see Outside the frame); and friends lying by message, and check-up calls that "kinda of got depressing" ().

Phones and games come between people in company: with everyone on their phones at a meal, "it kind of takes that connection away" (), and with friends playing FIFA, a game the interviewee dislikes, "you kind of have to disconnect with people" (). Dismay at social media's fakery is "one of despair because it’s not gonna change" (). Being without a phone makes one interviewee "feel so lost" (). One passage fits none of these roles: reading online about their symptoms "was just scaring me like all the time" ().

Alone or with someone

In , watching a Netflix series "no one watches" leaves "no one to talk to", while finding "the person that watches the same series" means "it kind of fills that loneliness" (). Screens used alone leave people still alone or bored in , , and (, , , ), but fill time or lift mood in , and (, , ); tells both, YouTube alone in their first year and Netflix on the laptop in their apartment now. In the control a phone gives over contact is both a relief and the means of the excuses that keep them in bed (, ); being without a phone, by contrast, is told as loss ().

By kind of technology

Social media is tied to negative feelings by people and to positive ones by . Messaging and calls run the other way: positive against negative. Gaming and streaming fall on both sides ( positive, negative). No passage was told as helping and harming at once in a way that could not be split ().

Outside the frame

Some of the strongest views about technology in these interviews are about other people, not the speaker's own mood, and so were not counted: people give such general views. One links social media comparison to loneliness among young people in general: "that leads them to be lonely" (); another sees social media as "just like drugs" for some people ().

There are doubts inside some accounts (). Asked how they feel about people on social media showing a different image from what they feel inside, one interviewee says "I don’t really feel anything about it" (), shortly after saying such posts make them feel "a little bit" worse (); of sitting in front of the telly for hours, the same interviewee says "I don’t do it personally" (). Of their own Snapchat posts, another reflects that "I could just enjoy their own company" (), and that "I felt the need to um for others to see and compare themselves with to make myself feel better" (). Straight after describing waiting by the phone for an invitation, another says that as an introvert "it’s a lot harder for me to kind of feel loneliness" (). One says that seeing what others have is "never a negative feeling", before describing Instagram making them feel not good enough (). One, asked how being left out without a phone makes them feel, names doubting whether anyone likes them and then says "But not in this case" (). And one gives friends a cover story for not being on social media ().

Some interviewees reject or reframe the interviewer's suggestion (). Asked whether friends gaming left them feeling left out, one says "it wasn’t more a feeling left out" (); another says that going round in circles at home is "not just a phone situation" (). One describes chatting on their phone as "a massive time-waster" that kept them up late, with no feeling attached (), the one effect of this kind ().

Limitations

This is a pilot of interviews, so most roles rest on a few people, and several on one person. The interviews were about loneliness, not technology, and interviewers sometimes raised social media themselves: Comparison drops from to people when prompted accounts are set aside, and Fakery from to . Each row records what a speaker says technology does to their own mood: a store of evidence about how it works, not a model of it (Powell, Copestake and Remnant 2024), and no measure of how much it does. One coder placed every passage, and a single reader checked the answer.

  • Entertainment and Keeping in touch as the joint commonest positive roles ( each) rest on counting music where no device is named (, ) as technology; read the other way, Entertainment falls below Keeping in touch, which becomes the single commonest role, and Comfort rests on alone.
  • That is the one person for whom technology only lifts mood () rests on not reading as a role their remark that since starting work "Whenever you message your friends, they’re busy, they can’t reply back", which they follow, when asked, with "It’s really sad" (); read as a negative role, nobody describes technology only lifting their mood.
  • Comparison's unprompted count () rests on how follow-up questions are marked: 's account is marked unprompted because they raised social media first, though the interviewer's question named it, while 's answers to questions about social media, which they had written on their sheet, are marked prompted; marked alike either way, the unprompted count would move by one person, down or up.

Annexes

How this report was written

What was read. Rubicon read 12 of the 48 documents in full, chosen by name. The counts below are of people, one document each.

Coding. It then marked every passage that bears on the question and recorded which side of the respondent's mood the technology bears on in this passage, which kind of technology the passage is about, whether the interviewer raised technology or social media in the question this passage answers, so the respondent did not bring it up themselves and what the technology does to or for the respondent's own feeling in this passage, as one specific thing with its direction, in close to the respondent's own words, such as 'seeing friends' posts makes me feel left out' or 'video calls with family keep me feeling close'. It also marked every passage that bears on the question and recorded why the passage bears on the question but falls outside its frame and one sentence on what the passage shows and why it falls outside the frame. It grouped the answers of role label into themes, which became a codebook, and placed each passage under one of them.

Checking. A separate reader then read the answer against the passages it cites and the documents, and checked every sentence and quotation, so the coding and the answer in this report are the corrected ones, counted again after the check.

Counting. Code brought together, for each document, everything coded in any of its passages and documents, and recorded whether any passage was coded mood positive and whether any passage was coded mood negative. People were then counted in 6 tables, compared by these codings. The annex below gives each.

Claims. The writer tagged 3 key claims that rest on no count, as each number is tagged: each names the passages for it and against it, how they would be found again and why they bear it out, and code checked that every passage named is one the coding holds.

Writing and checks. Rubicon wrote the answer from these counts, citing for each finding the passages it rests on. Every number in the answer, 44 in all, was computed directly from the coded passages rather than written by the AI, and all 100 coded passages were found word for word in their documents; every quotation in the answer, 48 in all, was found in the documents.

The workflow x-ray beside Step by step, below, draws the same procedure, a box for each stage and what it made.

Step by step

The analysis was written down as a workflow before it was counted: what to look for, how to code it, what to count. It was then counted directly from the coded passages rather than by the AI, so anyone can check a number, and another coder can follow the same definitions and code the interviews afresh.

The instruction a second coder would follow
Read the interview transcript. Interviewer turns are marked "I:" or "Interviewer:" and the respondent's "R:", "Interviewee:" or "Respondent:". Find every passage where the respondent ties a technology to a feeling of their own, positive or negative, including feeling lonely, left out, connected or supported. Technology covers social media (Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok, Facebook, Twitter, YouTube as a platform people post on), messaging apps, phone and video calls, gaming, streaming and watching video, and the internet or phone in general. Any role counts: the technology starting the feeling, keeping it going, easing it or lifting it. Give one row per distinct role in a passage; where one passage ties technology to two different feelings or in two different ways, give two rows. Quote the respondent's own words exactly, enough to show both the technology and the feeling, and never the interviewer's words. Do not code: feelings the interviewer suggests that the respondent does not take up; feelings the respondent attributes to other people; general remarks about social media, phones or "people these days" that the respondent does not apply to their own feelings; mentions of technology with no feeling of the respondent's attached; purely hypothetical feelings.
Role label

What the technology does to or for the respondent's own feeling in this passage, as one specific thing with its direction, in close to the respondent's own words, such as 'seeing friends' posts makes me feel left out' or 'video calls with family keep me feeling close'. Name the role, not just the technology or the feeling.

Mood

Which side of the respondent's mood the technology bears on in this passage.

CodeMeansCountsDoes not count
The technology lifts or eases the respondent's mood: they feel better, connected, supported, entertained, calmer or less lonely because of it.Feeling less lonely through messaging; enjoying gaming with friends; comfort from videos.A passage where the same use also leaves them feeling worse goes to mixed.
The technology starts, keeps going or worsens a negative feeling of the respondent's: lonely, left out, inadequate, anxious, low, isolated, envious.Feeling left out seeing posts; feeling lonelier after scrolling; anxiety about replies.Technology that eases a negative feeling goes to positive.
MixedThe respondent says in the same passage that the same use both helps and harms their mood, or that it helps in one way and hurts in another, and the two cannot be split into separate rows.'It keeps me in touch but it also makes me feel more alone.' when told as one inseparable point.Where the two sides are separable statements, code two rows, one positive and one negative.
Medium

Which kind of technology the passage is about.

CodeMeansCountsDoes not count
Platforms where people post and see others' posts: Instagram, Snapchat stories, TikTok, Facebook, Twitter, YouTube as a feed.Seeing posts, likes, followers, scrolling a feed.Private one-to-one or group messages go to messaging_calls, even on the same app.
Direct contact with particular people: texting, WhatsApp, direct messages, group chats, phone calls, FaceTime or video calls.Texting a friend, calling family abroad, a group chat.Public posts go to social_media.
Playing games (alone or online with others), watching TV, films, Netflix or YouTube videos for entertainment, listening to music on a device.Online gaming with friends, binge-watching, music.Posting or reading a feed goes to social_media.
The phone or internet in general, or a technology that fits none of the above, such as online dating or online learning.'Being on my phone all the time', the internet generally, dating apps.Anything that fits one of the three kinds above.
Prompted

yes where the interviewer raised technology or social media in the question this passage answers (or in the immediately preceding exchange), so the respondent did not bring it up themselves; no where the respondent brought technology up unprompted.

Coding: Off

one row for each passage that fits; 22 rows.

The instruction a second coder would follow
Read the interview transcript. Find passages that bear on how technology and social media relate to the respondent's own mood but that fall outside a coding of the respondent's own feelings tied to technology: general views about technology and other people, doubts or contradictions in the respondent's own account of technology and mood, suggestions by the interviewer about technology and feelings that the respondent rejects, and effects of technology on something other than mood. Quote the respondent's own words exactly.
Kind

Why the passage bears on the question but falls outside its frame.

CodeMeansCountsDoes not count
A view about what technology does to people in general, which the respondent does not apply to their own feelings in that passage.'Girls aspire to look a certain way'; 'we're all glued to our phones'.A general remark the respondent applies to their own feeling in the same passage is coded as a role, not here.
Something in the respondent's own account that cuts against or qualifies a role they describe elsewhere, such as saying they feel nothing about something they earlier said made them feel worse.Contradictions, second thoughts, cover stories.A plain change of topic.
The interviewer suggests a feeling or role of technology and the respondent declines or reframes it.'It wasn't more a feeling left out'.Minimal assent, which is neither coded here nor as a role.
An effect of technology on the respondent's time, sleep, work or relationships, with no feeling of theirs attached.Losing sleep to messaging.An effect with a stated feeling, which is a role.
Point

One sentence on what the passage shows and why it falls outside the frame.

What the grouping merged, split or left alone

Each item keeps one side of mood, since the question keeps positive and negative apart. Music was kept apart as comfort where the speaker turns to it when low, and as entertainment where it simply lifts the mood. Seeing that one is left out was kept apart from general comparison, because the first is about a particular event the speaker missed and the second about their standing against others. Screens coming between people in company was kept apart from screens failing to fill time alone. One label, a health scare from reading online, fits no role and is left unplaced.

  • Contact with a particular person through a call, a message or a shared series is told mostly as easing loneliness, while watching or playing alone is told both ways: as failing to fill the gap and as filling time or lifting mood.

Changes to rows

1. Removed c_tech.n8wph (I17, Empty filler, gaming_streaming, negative): "I know if I sit there and watch telly and doce- and chill all day and be lazy, then I know that I’m gonna feel worse about myself." Read in context it is conditional and expected only, and follows "Well, I don’t do it personally, but other people, I feel like it could be quite sad." The coding prompt excludes purely hypothetical feelings. I17 stays in Empty filler through c_tech.we6xs; t_medium[gaming_streaming,negative] falls from 6 to 5. Its label was removed from the Empty filler item. 2. Reworded c_off.v3e9u (I17, doubt): the point said the interviewer asked how curated images made them feel. The question was "And how do you feel about that", about people on social media showing an image different from what they feel; the point now says so. 3. k.connect: the reading said screens "lift mood when they connect the person to someone, and fail or lower it when they stand in for company". The passages do not bear it out: six people describe screens used alone lifting mood (the Entertainment rows of I04, I06, I17, I24, I28, I42), including I28's Netflix alone in their apartment (c_tech.3dcpm-2), which the reading left out. Rewritten as: contact with a particular person is told mostly as easing loneliness (against: I04, I42 messages and calls that hurt), and screens used alone are told both ways. 4. k.measure: "against" listed positive social media rows, which do not go against a claim about how social media lowers mood. Replaced by the negative social media rows that are not about a measure (I04 fakery; I28 fear of judgement; I42 fakery and false character; I43 browsing and Instagram in company), and the claim narrowed to "most of the negative accounts" (five of the seven people). 5. k.control: rested partly on I28's rows, where the speaker keeps off social media, which is not control that technology gives. Restricted to I37, with I07's managing of their feed as a further case of relief.

Narrow judgements
  • Most tie technology to both sides (t_sides[yes,yes], 9 of 12). Rests on each person's having at least one row on each side. Weakest: I43's only positive row (c_tech.rhah4, said of "you"); read the other way it is 8 of 12, still most. Stands.
  • One person only lifted (t_sides[yes,no], I29). Rests on not reading I29's unanswered messages as a role. A fair call either way; read as a role, the cell is 0. Limitations line added.
  • Commonest positive roles, Keeping in touch and Entertainment at 6 each (t_role). Rests on counting music without a named device (I06, I24 Entertainment; I06 Comfort). Read the other way, Entertainment falls to 4. Limitations line added.
  • Commonest negative roles, Comparison and Empty filler at 5 each. Rests on I37's TV models counting as technology and on I42's games boring them (c_tech.56ffx) counting as mood. Either flip leaves the other as single commonest, but both still head the negative roles. Not added.
  • Keeping in touch most often unprompted (6 against 4). Would need two calls to flip together; neither is fair. Stands.
  • Comparison unprompted (4). Rests on how follow-up questions naming technology the speaker had raised are marked: I17 marked no, I07 marked yes. Marked alike, it is 3 or 5. Limitations line added. The rows were left as coded because the definition supports either reading.
  • Most negative social media accounts are about a measure (k.measure, five of seven people). One fair flip (I42's unsure Facebook) leaves four of seven. Stands.
  • Contact eases, alone cuts both ways (k.connect, as corrected). Descriptive of rows on each side; stands. The earlier reading was wrong, not narrow, and was corrected.
  • Messaging runs positive (6 against 4) and social media negative (7 against 4). Recoding I37's social network chats as social media would leave messaging positive at 6 and raise social media positive to 5; both still stand.

What next

For the evaluator: Treat this report as a draft. Before it is final, make sense of it with the people it concerns, such as programme staff and participants: whether the findings ring true, what they leave out, and what to do about them. You can then use the Rubicon plugin to work their responses back into a revised answer.

For evaluation commissioners: Parallel to this report is a zip file (in-the-12-pilot-interviews-i04-i06-i07-i17-i18-i24-2026-10-20-9d3132de.zip), saved in the same folder, which contains the whole run: the documents, the coded passages and the workflow that recounts every number. Its fingerprint, under How this report was written, ties it to this report: change a file in either and they no longer match. With it, anyone can check every number against the coded passages, and code the documents again to the same definitions without Rubicon or any other particular software. A fresh coding will not reproduce this report word for word, because AI models are unpredictable, but it should come close.

🔥 Carbon cost of this report: Between 0.039 and 7.2 km driven in an average UK family car

Making this report used between 51.9 and 9586 watt-hours of electricity, which is the carbon of driving an average UK family car for that distance. A ballpark only: Anthropic publishes no energy figures, and the run, made in the evaluator's own Claude, records no token counts, so the estimate is made from the run's size. The 48 documents were read in full once by each of the 2 coding steps, by the second coder and by the check, and the writer read the tables; everything the run wrote counts as output. That comes to about 2,435,246 tokens read and 45,444 written, at 4 characters a token.

  • High: 0.39 Wh per thousand tokens read and 1.95 per thousand written, with what was read counted 10 times over for the agent's own overhead. Simon P. Couch, 'Electricity use of AI coding agents', 20 January 2026, https://simonpcouch.com/blog/2026-01-20-cc-impact/: about 390 Wh per million input tokens and 1,950 per million output tokens for Claude Opus, back-solved from Epoch AI's estimate for a 100,000-token prompt with output at five times the input rate, as Anthropic's prices are. The author calls them napkin maths. Our assumption, not a measurement: an agent re-sends its instructions, earlier turns and tool output with every request, so it reads far more than the documents themselves. The low case counts only what was read and written; the high case counts what was read ten times over.
  • Low: the same rates divided by 20, what was read counted once. Oviedo et al., 'Energy use of AI inference, efficiency pathways, and test-time scaling', arXiv:2509.20241: a median 0.31 Wh per query for frontier models, and widely cited estimates overstated by 4 to 20 times. The low case takes the high case's rates divided by the top of that range.
  • 0.124 kg CO2e per kWh. DESNZ greenhouse gas reporting conversion factors, UK grid electricity, 2024.
  • 0.16601 kg CO2e per km. DESNZ greenhouse gas reporting conversion factors, average car of unknown fuel, 2024.
